//: Who may touch what, written down BEFORE anyone starts. Two parcels claiming one file is the failure this file exists to prevent, and it costs one second to catch here instead of four hours in a merge. Read docs/parallel-dev.md first — it carries the brief to paste and the rule about not committing while agents are still typing.
//seams: Files everything needs. A parcel may ADD up to three lines to one of these and delete none, and must declare which lines up front. Two one-line additions merge by keeping both; two thirty-line edits merge into something nobody can verify. TWO STATED EXCEPTIONS, because the three-line grammar would make them unusable: scripts/build-kb.ts admits one appended Corpus const plus this door's name on the CORPORA line, and shared/roster.ts admits one whole appended agent entry. Both are appends at the end of a list, which is the shape that merges.
//frozen: Nobody edits these during a parallel run. A change here invalidates every parcel at once.
//alone: Parcels marked runAlone touch the room, the panel or the shell — everything reads those, and two agents in them at once produce a merge nobody can check. One agent, let it finish, then start the others.
//order: Three at a time, and NEVER two doors in the same wave — every door appends a Corpus const to scripts/build-kb.ts and a name to its CORPORA line, and they share one working tree. Wave 1: spend-limits, door-linkedin-ads, favicon-and-social. Wave 2: door-linkedin-automation, llms-txt, legal-name-display. Wave 3: door-ai-builds, payment-link. Then the runAlone ones, one after another. And do not let two agents run `npm run verify` at the same moment: vite empties dist/ on every build, so a concurrent build reads a directory another one is deleting. Ask them to report and run it yourself, or stagger it.

spend-limits.why: An agent reply costs about a quarter of a cent and a human conversation about three. Two agents answering each other cost about $4 an hour on this model — which is not frightening, and that is the danger: left running it is $104 a day and nobody notices, because nothing alarming happens at $4.
spend-limits.done: READ docs/OPENAI-SDK-NOTES.md first: the token-accounting recipe is already written there, so do not re-derive it. Today AgentStreamChunk carries only delta, citations and error, and create() sets no stream_options — so no token count, dollar figure or model name reaches the caller at all, and a cost log written today would be invented. The seam above is what makes the numbers exist. Then three independent bounds, because each fails differently: a count of turns per room, a clock that stops an agent after N minutes of activity, and a budget in money per room per month, warned at 80% and paused at 100%. One cost event per turn — room, agent, model, tokens in, tokens out, dollars — and nothing more. The count is taken atomically BEFORE the model call, so two messages arriving together cannot both pass. ON THE AGENT-REPLIES-TO-AGENT INVARIANT: check before you test it. POST /api/workspaces/:token/messages hard-codes authorKind "visitor" and resolveAgent takes no author argument, so a server-authored message cannot currently reach the reply path at all — the invariant holds by construction rather than by a rule. Say which it is in your report, and write the test against what the code actually does.

rented-accounts-inventory.//key: FLYGEN_API_KEY is in .env.local, which .gitignore covers. Read it from process.env. It must never appear in a tracked file, a test fixture, a log line, an error message, or anything the client receives.
rented-accounts-inventory.why: Whoever runs a boosting engagement needs to know what capacity exists and what state each unit is in — live, restricted, under appeal, rental ending. The Top-Voice contract now commits us to appealing a restriction and replacing the account if the appeal fails, and the room is where that sequence should be visible to the person managing it.
rented-accounts-inventory.done:
THEY ARE CALLED BOOSTERS, AND THEY ARE CAPACITY, NOT PEOPLE.

Never a room member: no avatar, no badge, no presence, no entry in the member rail or the @mention list. A
separate panel that reads like an inventory. The reason is in our own contract — terms.tsx section 6 says a
rented account "is not your employee, your colleague, or a person endorsing you, and you should not describe it
as one" — and the member rail prints who pays whom under every name, so an account listed there tells a client a
person is on their team when none is.

NAMING. A stable call sign per booster, assigned from a fixed list and never regenerated: `Booster 03 · Basalt`.
Numbers for order, one call sign for recall. Draw the call signs from a register of THINGS — minerals, stars,
weather, rivers — and NOT from people's names, actors, or characters.

  Two reasons, and the first is the load-bearing one. The API's `name` field is the real name of the real person
  whose account is rented. It is third-party personal data and it must never reach a room, a log or a client:
  this is the same rule Top-Voice's MEMBER_DATA_EXPORT switch exists to enforce. A call sign is what makes that
  possible while keeping the unit recognisable.

  The second: a human-sounding label recreates the exact confusion the panel exists to avoid. "Vito Corleone"
  in a room reads as a colleague; "Booster 03 · Basalt" cannot. A famous person's name also attaches a living
  individual to an account-rental operation without their knowledge.

  Map the call sign from the account id deterministically, so the same booster keeps the same name across
  restarts and no mapping has to be stored.

WHAT MAY LEAVE THE SERVER — an allowlist, not a blocklist, so a field flygen adds later cannot leak by default.
The room sees exactly: the call sign, the number, the state, the proxy's `location` (a country code, which is
operationally useful and identifies nobody), and the rental end date if the API ever exposes one.

  Dropped in server/flygen.ts before anything else touches the object: `name`, `email`, `password`,
  `twoFactorSecret`, `twoFactorSecretExpirationTime`, `description`, and the whole `proxy` object except
  `location`. Build the projection by naming the fields you keep — never by deleting the ones you don't.

NEVER PERSIST THE RAW RESPONSE. Not to the database, not to a file, not to a log, not in an error. The rate
limit is 20 requests per minute, so a cache is needed — cache the REDACTED projection only, and let the raw
response go out of scope in the same function that fetched it. A cached password is a stored password.

READ-ONLY. Fetch and display. This parcel does not rent, release, sign in, appeal, retry, or compute a TOTP
code, and it exposes no route that could. The docs explain how to generate 2FA codes; that is not this parcel's
business and no code for it belongs here.

TESTS, server-side and therefore mandatory:
  - the projection carries none of the seven dropped fields, asserted field by field against a fixture shaped
    like the documented response, with obviously-fake credentials in it;
  - a booster never appears in the members list or the mention list;
  - the same account id always yields the same call sign;
  - a 401, a 429 and a timeout each render the panel as "not available" rather than as an empty inventory —
    an empty list reads as "no boosters", which is a different fact from "we could not ask";
  - the API key appears in no response body and no thrown error.
rented-accounts-inventory.//api: GET https://api.flygen.in/api/m2m/accounts — Bearer token, 20 requests per minute per token, 429 beyond that. It returns EVERY field inline, credentials included: id, name, email, password, description, twoFactorSecret, twoFactorSecretExpirationTime, and proxy { host, port, username, password, mode, location, url }. There is no separate credentials call and no way to ask for less, so the redaction below is the only thing between that payload and a browser.

room-identity-binding.//depends: Read docs/pricing-spec.md — this parcel is the second half of its access ladder.
room-identity-binding.why: Three levels of access to the agents: a sold allowance with nobody signed in, more when signed in, and — the moment a visitor starts pasting links to their own accounts — a request to identify themselves for confidentiality. What is being offered is a convenience, not a gate: bind the room to their LinkedIn, or keep the link to it in WhatsApp so they can find it again.
room-identity-binding.done:
THREE LEVELS, and the third is the only one that asks for anything. Anonymous gets a bounded allowance.
Signed in gets more. When the visitor pastes a link to something of their own, the agent asks them to
identify themselves FOR CONFIDENTIALITY — because from that point the room contains their account, their
site, their numbers.

TWO ROUTES, and neither may be the only one:
  - LinkedIn, through the OFFICIAL API and its own consent screen. Nothing scraped, nothing session-based.
  - WhatsApp, through WAHA (https://waha.devlike.pro/), already running on another host: a link or a QR
    code opens WhatsApp with a pre-filled message carrying the address of their room, sent to us.

SAY WHAT IT IS FOR, in the strip itself, in one sentence: the room is bound to them so nobody else who
finds the link can read it, and the link lands in a place they will still have next week. Do not dress a
convenience as a security requirement, and do not imply LinkedIn endorses anything.

THE ROOM LINK IS A BEARER CREDENTIAL. It is already treated as one — robots.txt disallows /w/, the pages
carry noindex, and sitemap.xml leaves them out. Binding must NOT weaken that: identifying someone adds a
second fact about the room, it does not turn the token into a password. And a WhatsApp message carrying
the address means the credential now sits in a chat log, so say so plainly where the visitor chooses it.

WHAT MAY BE STORED. The minimum that answers "is this the same person": an opaque provider id and the
display name they chose to give. No phone number in a log, no LinkedIn access token beyond what the
binding needs, no contact list, nothing about anyone who is not the visitor.

TESTS: an unbound room keeps working at the anonymous allowance; a failed or abandoned identification
leaves the room exactly as it was rather than half-bound; the stored shape carries no token and no phone
number; and the WAHA host being down degrades to the LinkedIn route with a sentence saying so, never to a
dead button.
